title: Event-related transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation of auditory deviance
summary: This study investigates whether brief, low-intensity electrical stimulation of the outer left ear changes how people process unexpected sounds. Pupil size and the brain's electrical activity are measured at the same time. Healthy adults aged 20-30 attend two visits one week apart. One visit uses stimulation at an area of the outer ear, and the other uses the earlobe for comparison. Visit order is assigned randomly, and participants are not told during measurement which condition is active. At both visits they hear sound sequences and either count rare changes or perform a visual task while the sounds play in the background. Each visit lasts about two to two and a half hours. A total of 30 participants is planned. This is basic research, and no personal medical benefit is expected.
conditions: Healthy adults; basic research on local/global auditory deviance processing and modulation of attention and pupil responses by event-related taVNS.

interventions.name: Active event-related transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation at the left cymba conchae using Digitimer DS5. Biphasic pulses: 25 Hz, 250 µs, 1500-ms bursts; intensity individually calibrated within 0.1-5 mA and below the discomfort threshold. Each visit starts with 30 stimulation-only bursts

Sham stimulation at the left earlobe using Digitimer DS5, with the same individually calibrated pulse parameters and visit procedures as the active condition (25 Hz, 250 µs, 1500-ms bursts; intensity below the discomfort threshold). criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Healthy adults aged 20-30 years. German or English as a first or second language. Written informed consent before study procedures.
Exclusion criteria:
Acute or previous iritis; previous neurological or psychiatric conditions; relevant ocular disease, including previous eye surgery, glaucoma, pseudoexfoliation syndrome at the pupillary margin or lens, corneal disease, nonspheroidal pupils or relevant anisocoria; diabetes mellitus; use of centrally acting medication according to Table 2 of Kelbsch et al. (2019); multifocal contact lenses, mirrored lenses or highly reflective glasses components if these cannot be removed and adequate fixation without visual aids is not possible.
